steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on a Bayesian multilingual document model for zero-shot cross-lingual topic identification. It should explain the task and the usual approaches, discuss the problems with training big multilingual models and with classical topic models, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Zero-shot cross-lingual topic ID: what it is, why useful
- Common approach: multilingual model, then fine-tuning vs. embeddings + light classifier
- 1.1 Training multilingual models: data, cost, vocabulary, comparison problems
- Classical multilingual topic models
- 1.2 Contributions of the paper

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Zero-shot cross-lingual topic ID / document classification
  - classify target-language docs with classifier trained on source language(s)
  - useful when target languages have little or no labels for an in-language classifier
  - real-world applications (cite)
  - transfer experiments also test capabilities of the underlying multilingual LM
- Common approach
  - first train multilingual LM capturing semantic relations of words in context, language independent (cite)
  - then (i) fine-tune for classification with source labels (cite), or (ii) extract low-dim embeddings for source + target docs (cite); source embeddings + labels train a light-weight classifier, applied to target embeddings
  - fine-tuning inefficient: copy of whole model (or adapter layers) per source language and per task
  - embeddings: only one model + several light classifiers -> more practical
  - this paper: entirely about the latter scheme
- 1.1 Training multilingual models
  - recent works: LSTMs, transformers (cite), huge data e.g. 227M - 25B sentences (cite)
  - objectives depend on resources: parallel translations, bilingual dictionaries (cite), or monolingual texts
  - enormous compute (cite) -> need efficient alternatives
  - shared sub-word vocabulary across several (100) seed languages; equal representation needed to avoid bias from high resource languages
  - hard to extend to new languages with different orthography
  - fair comparison nearly impossible: no two models trained on same data; only downstream tasks compared, pre-training data quality/quantity ignored
  - web-data: down-stream data may have been seen in pre-training
  - surveys exist (cite)
- Classical multilingual topic models (cite)
  - suited for topic ID and document clustering; budget-friendly
  - evaluation datasets/tasks (cite) don't overlap with neural models -> hard to judge advantages
- 1.2 Contributions
  - multilingual Bayesian (MBay) model: simple, efficient, language-agnostic document (sentence) embeddings, robust linear classifiers for zero-shot cross-lingual topic ID
  - extend to new languages without re-training from scratch (continual learning), constrain only subset of parameters; implementation public
  - revisit zero-shot cross-lingual document classification: (i) evaluation shortcomings + robust alternative, (ii) 9 new languages from IndicNLP suite (cite) + existing 8 from MLDoc (cite), (iii) benchmark pre-trained models + ours on 17 languages (128 transfer directions), (iv) in depth analysis of downstream classifiers using the embeddings

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Zero-shot cross-lingual topic identification (ID), or document classification, is the task of classifying documents in target languages with a classifier that was trained on examples from one or more source language(s). This is mainly useful when the data in the target language(s) has few or no labels, so an in-language classifier can not be trained. These tasks also have real-world applications. Also, the cross-lingual transfer experiments can help to analyse and test what an underlying multilingual language model is capable of.

The usual approach is to first train a multilingual language model which tries to capture the semantic relations of words in context, independent of the language. This multilingual model can then be either (i) fine-tuned for the classification task using labelled examples from the source language(s), or (ii) used to extract low-dimensional embeddings (representations) of documents from both source and target languages. In the second case the embeddings from the source language(s) and the annotated labels are used to train a light-weight independent classifier for cross-lingual topic ID, and this classifier is then used to classify the embeddings from the target languages. The first approach with fine-tuning is not efficient, because you would need to keep a copy of the whole multilingual model (or a bunch of adapter layers) for every source language and for every down-stream task. The second approach, where language-agnostic document (sentence) embeddings are extracted, is more practical since it only needs one model and several light-weight downstream classifiers. This paper is completely focused on models, experiments and analysis for the second scheme, i.e. language agnostic document embeddings followed by a light-weight classifier.

## 1.1 Training multilingual models

- recent works: LSTMs, transformers, huge data e.g. 227M - 25B sentences
- objectives depend on resources: parallel translations, bilingual dictionaries, or monolingual texts
- enormous compute -> need efficient alternatives
- shared sub-word vocabulary across several (100) seed languages; language bias from high resource languages; hard to extend to new orthography
- fair comparison nearly impossible; only downstream tasks compared; down-stream data maybe seen in web pre-training
- surveys exist
- classical multilingual topic models: topic ID, clustering, budget-friendly, but datasets/tasks don't overlap with neural ones

## 1.2 Contributions of the paper

- MBay model for language-agnostic document (sentence) embeddings, robust linear classifiers
- easy extension to new languages (continual learning); implementation public
- revisit task: (i) evaluation shortcomings, (ii) 9 IndicNLP languages + 8 from MLDoc, (iii) benchmark on 17 languages (128 transfer directions), (iv) analysis of downstream classifiers

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Zero-shot cross-lingual topic identification (ID), or document classification, is the task of classifying documents in target languages with a classifier that was trained on examples from one or more source language(s). This is mainly useful when the data in the target language(s) has few or no labels, so an in-language classifier can not be trained. These tasks also have real-world applications. Also, the cross-lingual transfer experiments can help to analyse and test what an underlying multilingual language model is capable of.

The usual approach is to first train a multilingual language model which tries to capture the semantic relations of words in context, independent of the language. This multilingual model can then be either (i) fine-tuned for the classification task using labelled examples from the source language(s), or (ii) used to extract low-dimensional embeddings (representations) of documents from both source and target languages. In the second case the embeddings from the source language(s) and the annotated labels are used to train a light-weight independent classifier for cross-lingual topic ID, and this classifier is then used to classify the embeddings from the target languages. The first approach with fine-tuning is not efficient, because you would need to keep a copy of the whole multilingual model (or a bunch of adapter layers) for every source language and for every down-stream task. The second approach, where language-agnostic document (sentence) embeddings are extracted, is more practical since it only needs one model and several light-weight downstream classifiers. This paper is completely focused on models, experiments and analysis for the second scheme, i.e. language agnostic document embeddings followed by a light-weight classifier.

## 1.1 Training multilingual models

Most, if not all, recent works on multilingual representations for cross-lingual transfer rely on training LSTMs or transformers on huge amounts of data (e.g. 227M - 25B sentences). The pre-training objectives are different depending on what kind of resources are used for training the models. Briefly, some of them need parallel translations of sentences across multiple languages, while others rely on bilingual dictionaries or only on monolingual texts covering several languages. Training these large multilingual language models needs enormous computational resources, so there is a need for alternatives that are computationally efficient. Most of the large multilingual models share a vocabulary of sub-word units across several (100) seed languages. Care has to be taken so that all the languages are equally represented in the shared (sub-)word vocabulary, otherwise there is a language bias from the high resource languages. This design choice also makes it hard to extend these models to newer languages which have a different orthography. It is nearly impossible to compare these language models fairly, because no two models are trained on exactly the same data. The comparisons are only done on the downstream tasks and the effect of the quality and quantity of the pre-training data is ignored. When training on large amounts of web-data, it is possible that some of the down-stream data was already seen during pre-training. Extensive surveys of these models and approaches are available.

Apart from the neural models, there is also work on classical multilingual topic models, which can be used for topic ID and document clustering. These models are budget-friendly when it comes to computation, but the downstream evaluation datasets and tasks of the neural and the classical models do not overlap, so it is hard to tell what the advantages of the classical models over the neural ones are.

## 1.2 Contributions of the paper

- We propose a multilingual Bayesian (MBay) model which is simple but efficient, for learning language-agnostic document (sentence) embeddings, and which lets us train robust downstream linear classifiers for zero-shot cross-lingual topic ID.

- The model can easily be extended to newer languages without having to re-train from scratch (continual learning), and only a subset of the existing parameters is constrained, which keeps it computation-budget-friendly. Our implementation is public.

- We re-visit the zero-shot cross-lingual document classification task and contribute the following: (i) we identify shortcomings in the evaluation and propose a robust alternative, (ii) we set up and evaluate zero-shot transfer systems on a new set of 9 languages from the IndicNLP suite, in addition to the existing 8 from MLDoc, (iii) we benchmark several pre-trained models and also the proposed model on the revised datasets which cover 17 languages (128 transfer directions), and (iv) we give an in depth analysis of the downstream classification systems that can best make use of the language-agnostic document (sentence) embeddings from various models.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Zero-shot cross-lingual topic identification (ID), or document classification, aims to classify documents from target languages using a classifier trained on examples from one or more source language(s). This is mainly useful in scenarios where the data from the target language(s) have little or no labels for training an in-language classifier. Such tasks also have real-world applications [1]. Furthermore, cross-lingual transfer experiments can also help to analyse and test the capabilities of an underlying multilingual language model.

The common approach is to first train a multilingual language model that aims to capture the semantic relations of words in context, independent of the language [2,3,4,5,6]. Such a model can later be either (i) fine-tuned for the classification [7] task using labelled examples from the source language(s), or (ii) used to extract low-dimensional embeddings (representations) for documents from both source and target languages [8]; the source-language embeddings together with the annotated labels are then used to train a light-weight independent classifier for cross-lingual topic ID, which is then applied to the embeddings from the target languages. The former approach, relying on fine-tuning, is not efficient as it requires keeping a copy of the entire multilingual model (or a bunch of adapter layers) for every source language and every down-stream task. The latter approach of extracting language-agnostic document (sentence) embeddings is more practical, as it requires only one model and several light-weight downstream classifiers. This paper focuses entirely on models, experiments and analysis related to the latter scheme, relying on language agnostic document embeddings followed by a light-weight classifier.

## 1.1 Training multilingual models

Most, if not all, of the recent works in multilingual representations for cross-lingual transfer have relied on training LSTMs [9,3] or transformers [10,5] with huge amounts of data (e.g. 227M - 25B sentences) [10,7]. The pre-training objectives vary depending on the kind of resources used for training such models. In brief, some require parallel translations of sentences across multiple languages, while others rely on bilingual dictionaries [2] or just on monolingual texts covering several languages. Training these large multilingual language models requires enormous computational resources [11], so there is a need for computationally efficient alternatives. Most of the large multilingual models share a vocabulary of sub-word units across several (100) seed languages, and care must be taken that all languages are equally represented in the shared (sub-)word vocabulary to avoid a language bias from the high resource languages. Such a design choice also makes it challenging to extend these models to newer languages with a different orthography. A fair comparison among these language models is nearly impossible, as no two models are trained on exactly the same data; comparisons are made only on downstream tasks, ignoring the effect of the quality and quantity of pre-training data. When training on large amounts of web-data, some of the down-stream data could also have been seen during pre-training. An extensive survey of the aforementioned models and approaches can be found in [12,13].

In contrast to the neural models, there is also work on classical multilingual topic models [14,15], which are suitable for topic ID and document clustering. While these models are budget-friendly in terms of computation, the downstream evaluation datasets and tasks [16,17,18] of neural and classical models do not overlap, so it is difficult to ascertain the advantages of the latter over the former.

## 1.2 Contributions of the paper

- We propose a simple yet efficient multilingual Bayesian (MBay) model for learning language-agnostic document (sentence) embeddings, which enables training robust downstream linear classifiers for zero-shot cross-lingual topic ID.

- The proposed model can easily be extended to newer languages without re-training from scratch (continual learning), constraining only a subset of the existing parameters, which makes it computation-budget-friendly. Our implementation is public.

- We re-visit the zero-shot cross-lingual document classification task and make the following contributions: (i) we identify shortcomings in the evaluation and propose a robust alternative, (ii) we set up and evaluate zero-shot transfer systems on a new set of 9 languages from the IndicNLP suite [17], in addition to the existing 8 from MLDoc [16], (iii) we benchmark several pre-trained models, as well as the proposed model, on the revised datasets covering 17 languages (128 transfer directions), and (iv) we provide an in depth analysis of the downstream classification systems that can best make use of the language-agnostic document (sentence) embeddings from various models.
